disability.title: How to cope with physical limitations?
disability.description: This article explores how physical limitations affect mental well-being, highlighting the role of cognitive distortions in how we perceive our own abilities. Through the story of Anna, who experienced depression after her husband became disabled, we see the path to emotional recovery through cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and a shift in life values. The article concludes with a reflection on the importance of focusing on possibilities rather than limitations, encouraging readers to re-evaluate their views on happiness and self-fulfillment.

texts: Physical limitations are one category of problems perceived as “real”.
People facing various limitations due to age or disability—for example, after an amputation—often fear that these changes will prevent them from experiencing happiness.
Disability is a massive stressor. This is especially true when it happens suddenly, such as following a road accident.
In that moment, a person faces the reality of loss: for instance, a spinal cord injury might mean they can no longer walk.
A normal life and a familiar worldview can shatter overnight, replaced by pain, fear, and confusion.
The process of adapting to new life circumstances involves various emotions and states, which psychologists often divide into stages: denial, depression, acceptance, and so on.
Some people may “get stuck” in one stage for years, lacking the strength to move to the next, while others might “skip” certain stages entirely.
Beyond the fact that every individual perceives their physical limitations differently, much also depends on their loved ones, the support they receive, and many other factors.
<important>Friends and relatives usually show understanding and sympathy, believing this is the right response. However, such support can sometimes have the opposite effect.</important>
Emotional suffering is often caused not by physical limitations themselves, but by cognitive distortions.

In these situations, compassion can sometimes backfire, intensifying self-pity and despair, and reinforcing the belief that a person with a disability is destined to experience less joy and satisfaction in life than others.
Conversely, when those affected and their loved ones learn to work through these distortions, they often find a more fulfilling and joyful emotional life.
Take Anna, for example—a 35-year-old married mother of two, who began experiencing symptoms of depression around the time her husband’s right leg was paralyzed due to a spinal injury.
For five years, she searched for ways to ease her growing despair, including outpatient and inpatient treatment, antidepressants, and even electroconvulsive therapy, but to no avail.
By the time Anna sought help from a cognitive behavioral therapist, she was already in a deep depression and felt her problems were unsolvable.
Through tears, she spoke about the frustration of trying to cope with her husband’s reduced mobility: "Every time I see other couples doing things we can't, it becomes unbearably sad.
I watch families walking together, traveling, or riding bikes, and it hurts. It would be incredibly difficult for Roma and me to do those things.
They see it as perfectly natural and normal, just like we used to. I want so much to do the same, but we just can't."
Of course, we cannot deny that Anna and Roma’s problem is very real; they truly cannot do many of the things most of us can.
The same applies to the elderly, as well as to those who are blind, deaf, have amputations, or face many other physical limitations.
In fact, if you think about it, we all have some limitations. Does that mean we should all be deeply unhappy?

<q author="Nick Vujicic">There are many things in life that are much worse than not having arms and legs. Fear is one of them. It is impossible to live life to the fullest if every decision you make is driven by fear.</q>

test.question: Which cognitive distortion was most prevalent in Anna’s thinking?

texts: Of course, the cognitive distortion that led to Anna’s emotional suffering and depression was a mental filter.
She fixated on what was unavailable to her, while ignoring many opportunities to do things together with her husband. This explains her sense of emptiness and joylessness.
The solution turned out to be surprisingly simple: together with her psychologist, she made a list of everything Anna and Roman could do together.
In this way, instead of focusing only on what they couldn’t do, they began to see opportunities for spending time together. Let’s look at their dialogue:
<dialog psy="true">So, Anna, what do you and your husband do, or could do, together?</dialog>
<dialog>Well, we still enjoy each other’s company. We go out to dinner together, and we are a great support for one another.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Wonderful, what else?</dialog>
<dialog>Sometimes we drive around the city or go out to the countryside, play board games, watch movies, read and discuss books, invite friends over, and cook lunch together.</dialog>

<dialog psy="true">You see, in less than a minute, you’ve already listed five things you can do together. Let’s say I gave you an assignment to continue this list before our next session. How many more items do you think you could add?</dialog>
<dialog>I think a lot. I could probably think of things we’ve never done before. Maybe something unusual, like skydiving.</dialog>

<dialog psy="true">That’s right, of course. You might be able to add more extreme activities. Keep in mind that you and your husband could do many of the things you gave up on simply because you assumed they were impossible.</dialog>

<dialog psy="true">For example, you said you couldn’t go to the seaside and walk on the beach, but you also mentioned how much you wanted to go swimming. Perhaps you could plan a trip and choose a more secluded spot so you don’t feel self-conscious?</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">If I were at the beach and saw you and Roman, his physical disability wouldn’t bother me at all. What do you think?</dialog>
<dialog>I’m surprised, but that thought doesn’t seem so impossible now. It feels quite realistic, and I feel a great surge of energy and inspiration from these thoughts.</dialog>
Some people might not believe that such a difficult problem can be solved, or that depression like Anna’s can lift after working on thoughts and beliefs.
Nevertheless, by the end of therapy, Anna noted that her negative emotions had completely vanished, and she said she felt better than she had in years.

To maintain this progress, she will, of course, need to continue working hard on herself—working through her thoughts and changing her thinking habits—but she is ready and willing, which is the most important part of treating depression.

<important>It is important to understand that we are by no means dismissing physical limitations. However, we understand—and we want you to understand—how vital it is in these difficult circumstances to learn to focus on what you are capable of doing, rather than concentrating on what you cannot do.</important>
For example, imagine you really want to fly to the Moon.

If you constantly thought about how unlikely it is that you’ll fly to the Moon—since you aren’t an astronaut, your health isn’t good enough, you don’t have enough money, or you aren’t as young as you used to be—it would likely leave you feeling very frustrated.
However, there are many other things you can do, and if you focus on them, you will feel much happier.

disease.title: Depression and a Terminal Diagnosis
disease.description: This article explores the emotional and psychological challenges people face after receiving a serious diagnosis, highlighting how difficult it can be to communicate these experiences to others. It tells the story of Olga, whose life changed drastically following a cancer scare, and how she worked through depression and a loss of meaning with the help of a psychologist. Ultimately, Olga came to realize her inherent personal value and the importance of small achievements, which helped her rebuild her self-esteem and shift her emotional state despite her physical suffering.

texts: What happens to a person when they learn they have a serious, potentially life-threatening illness? Many people face such trials, yet explaining what they feel to someone who is healthy can seem like an incredibly difficult task.
<q author="Jules Renard">Your illness does not define you. It is your strength and courage in facing it that defines you.</q>
Stories of people facing serious illness are often the basis for novels or films. In cinema, these plots might take a comedic form, but in reality, things are much more complex.
Regardless of the severity or duration of the illness, a “terminal diagnosis” always hits like an explosion or a lightning strike.

A person facing a terminal diagnosis may experience reactive depression. Reactive depression is a rapidly developing mental health condition that arises in response to traumatic events or intense stress.
In this state, a person may constantly experience fear, anxiety, apathy, low mood, fatigue, insecurity, and suicidal thoughts, as well as issues with sleep and appetite.
<important>Many illnesses fundamentally change a person’s lifestyle. Someone who was once a healthy, active lover of travel and nature can overnight become unable to get out of bed.</important>
In such a state, they may be unable to use the bathroom or take a shower independently, let alone go for a simple walk.
Moreover, realizing how much time and energy their loved ones must spend on their care can make them feel like a burden.
Olga was 39 years old when her life changed drastically due to a cancer scare.

It felt as if life had come to a standstill; she felt cut off from her familiar reality. All her previous fears and anxieties seemed trivial and insignificant compared to the horror that had suddenly descended upon her.
When her worst fears were confirmed, it hit Olga and her family like a grenade blast.
In the months that followed, physical weakness plunged her into even deeper despondency.
Everything was made harder not just by the physical discomfort of the illness and chemotherapy, but by the need to give up activities that had been deeply meaningful to her.
Olga could no longer manage household chores as she once did (her husband took these over), and she had to give up her beloved work, hobbies, and long walks with friends.
<important>Given the reality of Olga’s situation, should her depression be considered inevitable?</important>
Through her work with a psychologist, she identified the automatic thoughts and unhelpful beliefs that were troubling her:
• I am not contributing to society
• I am not succeeding in my career
• I can no longer participate in active leisure
• I have become a burden to my husband
These thoughts triggered sadness, anger, frustration, and guilt—similar to the thoughts of physically healthy people experiencing depression.

The depression was caused not so much by the tumor itself, but by a negative mindset that undermined her sense of self-worth. By linking her personal value to her achievements, Olga was causing herself unnecessary suffering.
To her, cancer meant: “Your time is up! You are worth nothing now!”.
When Olga and her psychologist mapped out her personal “value” from birth to her projected lifespan, she saw that her inherent value remained unchanged, staying at 85% on a scale of 0 to 100%.
The psychologist also suggested she rate her productivity over a similar period.
She drew a curve showing that her productivity was low in childhood, peaked during adulthood, and then declined toward the present.

This led to an insight for Olga. First, she realized that even though her productivity had dropped due to illness, she continued to contribute to herself and her family through many small but important and valuable actions.
Only black-and-white thinking could have pushed her to believe that her contribution was zero.
Second, and more importantly, she realized that her personal value was constant and stable; it was an inherent truth, independent of her achievements.
<important>This understanding allowed her to realize that she doesn’t have to “earn” her human worth, and that even while weakened, she remains just as valuable.</important>

Realizing this fact significantly reduced her depressive symptoms. It didn’t remove the tumor, the pain, or the physical suffering, but it restored her wounded self-esteem and substantially changed her emotional state.
<q author="Nick Vujicic">Illness cannot steal your hope unless you let it.</q>

distortions.title: Reframing Your Thinking: Overcoming Depression by Understanding Cognitive Distortions
distortions.description: In this article, we explore how cognitive distortions contribute to the development and maintenance of depression, and why understanding these mechanisms is so vital. We offer practical ways to recognize and change negative thinking patterns to help improve your mental well-being. By diving deeper into the topic of cognitive distortions, you are taking an important step toward recovery and strengthening your mental well-being.

texts: In previous chapters, we’ve discussed how common depression symptoms are and how they impact our lives. You might have wondered: why do I feel so bad? Why does the future seem so hopeless? Let’s try to find the answer together.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has contributed immensely to our understanding of the nature of depression. Today, we know that negative emotions often arise as a result of a distorted, pessimistic perception of oneself, the world, and the future.

When someone experiences depression, their attention seems to tune into the negative: they notice bad events more often, interpret neutral ones in an unfavorable light, and either discount or overlook the good ones.
<q author="William James">The greatest discovery of my generation is that a person, by changing their internal attitudes, can change the external aspects of their life.</q>
At the core of a depressive state, there are almost always persistent unhelpful beliefs and distorted ways of thinking.
These irrational thoughts can be categorized. This is how we arrived at the concept of “cognitive distortions.”
Cognitive distortions manifest in different ways. For example:

A person makes broad conclusions based on single events: one mistake is perceived as proof of total incompetence, and one failure is seen as a sign that success is impossible. “I’ll never succeed” or “I’m useless” are common thoughts during depression.

People are also prone to grim predictions, convincing themselves in advance that the future will inevitably be bad. “I’ve already seen a psychologist and it didn’t help—so nothing ever will,” or “I’ll always be alone and unhappy.”
With this kind of internal dialogue, it is very difficult to maintain a good mood or a sense of hope.

<important>But there is supportive news: your thoughts can be the key to relieving your symptoms. By learning to notice and change unhelpful beliefs, you can influence your mood and well-being.</important>

test.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of “cognitive distortions” in the context of depression?
answers: A state of mental health that cannot be changed
Positive thinking patterns that help cope with depression
Irrational beliefs and thoughts that worsen a depressive state
Physical symptoms that arise as a result of depression

texts: It is important to learn how to notice your irrational thoughts and understand which type of cognitive distortion they belong to.
This will help you recognize unhelpful patterns early on, preventing them from taking root.
There are many cognitive distortions, and we have gathered the most important ones on a dedicated page in your automatic thought journal.
We recommend heading to that section to learn about each distortion in more detail—including all the material here would be too overwhelming.
Read the descriptions and dialogue examples to see how these distortions manifest in real life.
Try to notice if similar beliefs appear in your own thoughts, and begin to gently replace them with more realistic and helpful ones.
The topic of cognitive distortions is so significant that in the following chapters, we will dive deeper into the most common ones.
